posts.quote: FOUR BOARDS AND A COFFEE CAN OF BENT NAILS MADE THE FINEST TREE HOUSE IN THE COUNTY.
posts.caption: It started the day somebody found a stack of old boards behind the Hendersons' garage. By lunchtime we had Dad's hammer, a coffee can of nails we'd pulled out of a fence, and a plan nobody had written down. Half the nails went in crooked and the other half went into the yard. The ladder was three slats nailed straight into the trunk, and you didn't put your full weight on the middle one. It leaned a little to the left and the roof was a piece of tarp. We'd have told you it was the finest house in the county, and we'd have meant it.
posts.first:
Ours lasted three summers in the big maple out back before a storm took the roof. My brother and I signed our names on the underside of the floor with a nail. I'd bet money they're still up there.

posts.quote: FIVE PUSH BUTTONS ON THE DASHBOARD, AND DAD HAD EVERY ONE OF THEM SET TO A BALL GAME.
posts.caption: The car radio had five chrome buttons, and you didn't touch them. Dad set them himself, one station at a time, with the little knob and a lot of patience. Every one of them carried a ball game somewhere in the state, and on a summer night you could drive two hundred miles and never miss an inning. The announcer's voice would fade in and out as we passed through the hills, and Dad would lean toward the dash like that would help. Mom tried to sneak a music station onto button four once. It lasted exactly one trip to the grocery store.
posts.first:
Our station wagon had an AM radio with a dial light that glowed orange after dark. I fell asleep in the back seat to more extra innings than I can count. To this day a baseball game on the radio sounds like riding home at night.

posts.quote: "BECAUSE I SAID SO" WAS A COMPLETE SENTENCE, AND THERE WAS NO APPEALS COURT.
posts.caption: You'd ask why, because every kid has to ask why at least once. Why can't I go to Danny's? Why do I have to wear the brown shoes? Mom wouldn't even turn around from the stove. Four words came back over her shoulder, and that was the end of the hearing. No explanation, no second opinion, no going to ask Dad, because Dad would say the exact same four words. You'd stand there a second like you were thinking up an argument. Then you'd go put on the brown shoes.
posts.first:
I swore up and down I would never say it to my own kids. I made it to about my oldest's fifth birthday. It came out of my mouth in my mother's exact voice, and I had to sit down for a minute.

posts.quote: We called our friends' parents Mr. and Mrs. Their first names were a mystery we never once dared to solve.
posts.first:
I was twenty-five before I found out Mrs. Kowalski's name was Dorothy, and I still couldn't bring myself to say it. She'll always be Mrs. Kowalski to me. Some things you just don't outgrow.

posts.quote: THE FILMSTRIP PROJECTOR / WHEN IT BEEPED, YOU TURNED THE KNOB, AND EVERY KID IN CLASS WANTED THAT JOB
posts.caption: The teacher would pull down the screen, and the whole room perked up. Somebody got sent to roll the cart in, and somebody else got to work the knob. A record played along with a voice that sounded like a newscaster, and every so often it would beep. That beep was your cue to turn to the next frame. Miss it, and the whole class would yell at you at once. It was the most power a ten-year-old ever held, and we fought over it like it was the presidency.
posts.first:
I got picked to turn the knob exactly once in fourth grade. I was so nervous about missing the beep that I turned it early three times, and the whole filmstrip got ahead of the record. Mrs. Baker never picked me again.

posts.quote: WE LICKED A THOUSAND TRADING STAMPS TO GET ONE TOASTER, AND WE WERE PROUD OF THAT TOASTER.
posts.caption: Every trip to the grocery store came home with a strip of stamps in the bag. They went in a kitchen drawer until there were enough to make it worth getting out the books. Then the whole family sat at the table and licked and stuck, page after page, until your tongue tasted like glue for a week. Mom kept a catalog and had her heart set on something in it for months. When the books were finally full, it was a family outing to the redemption store. That toaster sat on our counter for fifteen years, and nobody ever forgot what it cost.
posts.first:
Mom saved up for a set of mixing bowls, and it took her most of a year. My job was the sponge in a saucer so we didn't have to lick them all. I thought I'd invented something.

posts.character: Crafts and homemaking (pie on the windowsill)
posts.quote: A PIE COOLING ON THE WINDOWSILL WAS AN OPEN INVITATION TO EVERY KID AND DOG ON THE STREET.
posts.caption: You could smell it from the end of the block. Somewhere a back window was open, and on the sill sat a cherry pie with steam still coming off the crust. Every kid in the neighborhood suddenly found a reason to walk past that house. The dogs didn't bother pretending. Mrs. Lindstrom would lean out and tell us it was for supper, and we'd nod like we understood. Then she'd sigh, cut it anyway, and hand out slices on paper napkins. I think she baked two on purpose and never said a word about it.
posts.first:
My grandmother made her crusts with lard and never once measured the flour. She'd set the pies on the back porch rail to cool, and the neighbor's beagle would sit underneath and stare at them like he was praying. She always saved him the crimped edges.

posts.character: Humor about today vs. then (air conditioning)
posts.quote: Our air conditioning was an open window, a box fan, and a cold washcloth on the back of your neck.
posts.first:
On the worst nights we'd drag our mattresses down to the living room floor in front of the fan. Mom would put a bowl of ice in front of it like that was going to save us. Honestly, I think it did a little.

posts.quote: THE SCISSORS GRINDER / HE RANG A BELL DOWN THE STREET, AND EVERY DULL KNIFE IN THE NEIGHBORHOOD CAME OUT TO MEET HIM
posts.caption: You heard him before you saw him. A hand bell, ringing slow and steady somewhere a couple of blocks over, and every mother on the street started opening drawers. He pushed a cart with a big grinding wheel he worked with a foot pedal. Out came the kitchen knives, the sewing shears, the garden clippers, and once in a while a lawnmower blade. He'd set up at the curb and sparks would fly off the stone while we kids stood back and watched like it was the Fourth of July. A few minutes later everything came back sharp enough to split a hair, and he'd ring his way on down the road.
posts.first:
Mom only trusted him with her good sewing scissors, and she stood right there the whole time he worked on them. He let me pump the pedal once while he held the blade. I told everybody at school I was learning a trade.

posts.quote: A PUSH MOWER AND A SATURDAY MORNING WERE GOOD FOR TWO DOLLARS AND A GLASS OF ICED TEA.
posts.caption: Nobody handed you spending money. If you wanted a new ball glove, you went door to door with the old reel mower clattering behind you. Mr. Pruitt paid a dollar and Mrs. Haley paid two, but you had to do her edges with the hand clippers. By noon your shirt was soaked and your arms were green to the elbow. Then somebody's wife would bring out a glass of iced tea with the ice already half gone, and you'd drink it standing on the porch steps. That glove cost me six Saturdays. I still have it.
posts.first:
I had five yards by the summer I turned twelve and kept every dollar in a cigar box under my bed. Dad made me sharpen the mower blades myself before he'd let me take it out. He said a man takes care of his tools, and that stuck.
